I had no retrieved literature to work from (the list was empty), so these hypotheses come from my prior knowledge of NAS-Bench-201 and are not checked against any data. They rest on three patterns:

- **Replacing `none` gains the most.** An edge that currently carries `none` has the most to gain from a real operation.
- **Strong parents gain less.** A cell that already has convolutions gains less from another one, and loses more when a good operation is removed.
- **Dead paths cancel an edit.** If a parent edge removes node 1 from the graph, edits to edges 2 and 4 stop mattering.
